passage: Ganga came into the grocery shop at closing time, still in her work apron. "Two years, Tushar. You said you'd share the stall, and I paid the advance on my own. Not a word from you." Tushar's first thought was to say he had been scared of losing his father's shop, but he shut his mouth and let her finish. When she stopped, he said, "I left you with the whole rent and the bad name, and I never called. That was wrong, and I'm sorry. I'm not asking you to say it's okay." Ganga folded her arms. "Then what are you asking?" "Nothing. But if you want, I'll pay back what you lost, in whatever pieces I can." She looked at the floor tiles, then left without answering. He locked the shutter slowly.

qa.q: What did Ganga say Tushar had promised about the stall?
qa.a: She said he had promised to share the stall.

qa.q: What was Tushar's first thought when Ganga confronted him, and what does staying quiet show?
qa.a: He wanted to explain that he had been scared of losing his father's shop, but he held back, which shows he chose to listen rather than defend himself.

qa.q: What made Tushar's apology better than an excuse would have been?
qa.a: He named what he did (leaving Ganga with the rent and the bad name, never calling), did not ask for forgiveness, and offered to pay back what she lost.

qa.q: How might Ganga see the moment when Tushar apologises?
qa.a: Ganga may still be angry and unsure, folding her arms and leaving without answering, which suggests forgiveness is hers to give in her own time.

grounding: Someone Tushar wronged comes with anger; he listens without defending, apologises specifically, offers repair and does not demand forgiveness.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,

Thank you for your message, even though it was hard to read. You're right to be angry.

Two years ago, when we built the inventory tool together, I presented it to the directors as mine. I didn't mention your name. I got the promotion. You got nothing, and you left the company a few months later.

I'm not going to explain why. There's no good reason. I was scared of being ordinary, and I took something that was yours.

I'm sorry for taking credit for your work, for staying silent when you asked about it, and for the months of doubt it caused you.

I don't expect forgiveness. If you ever want me to, I'll write to the directors and tell them the truth about who built it. I'll also give a reference to anyone you want.

Whether you reply or not is up to you. I'll respect either.

Mehak

qa.q: What did Mehak present to the directors as Mehak's own?
qa.a: The inventory tool Mehak and Jeevan built together.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling while writing to Jeevan?
qa.a: Mehak felt guilty and ashamed about taking credit, and ready to face Jeevan's anger without making excuses.

qa.q: What did Mehak do right in the apology?
qa.a: Mehak listened to Jeevan's anger, named exactly what happened without excuses, didn't demand forgiveness, and offered concrete repair like telling the directors the truth.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see the letter?
qa.a: Jeevan may still feel angry, but also validated that Mehak finally admitted the truth, and free to decide in Jeevan's own time.

grounding: The letter shows someone who wronged an old colleague responding to that anger by listening, apologising specifically, offering repair and leaving forgiveness to Jeevan.

passage:
"So I got this message from Swati last month. I'm Pranav, by the way, and this is the most embarrassing story I have.

Three years ago, we were close. Like, planning-a-trip close. Then I just stopped replying. No explanation. I was going through a bad patch and it was easier to disappear than to explain.

Her message was angry. 'You made me feel like I was nothing. I thought I'd done something wrong for a year.'

My first reflex was to defend myself. I was depressed, I was busy, whatever. I typed it and deleted it.

Instead I wrote, 'You're right. I disappeared without a word, and it wasn't anything you did. I'm really sorry for making you doubt yourself for so long.'

I didn't ask her to forgive me. I said if she ever wanted to talk it through, I'd listen.

She replied two weeks later. Just: 'Thanks for not making excuses.' That's all. And honestly, that's enough."

qa.q: How long ago did Pranav stop replying to Swati?
How did Pranav feel when he first read Swati's angry message?
qa.a: Pranav felt defensive, wanting to explain, and then guilty for the pain the silence had caused.

qa.q: What did Pranav do instead of defending himself?
qa.a: Pranav apologised specifically for disappearing and making Swati doubt herself, didn't demand forgiveness, and offered to listen if she wanted.

qa.q: How does Swati seem to see Pranav's apology?
qa.a: Swati appreciates that Pranav didn't make excuses, though she keeps her reply short and on her own terms.

grounding: The spoken account shows someone contacted in anger by a wronged old friend, listening without defending, apologising specifically and leaving forgiveness to her.
